title: Medium exam 5
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace two or three steps: process trees, globs against regular expressions, quoting, link counts, `tee`, `info` and `find -exec`.

questions.title: Showing the process tree
questions.text: Which pair of commands shows the processes with their parent and child relations drawn as a tree?

options.why: `ps aux` is a flat list; the tree needs the `f` option of `ps`.
Both give a list, one static and the other refreshed, without the hierarchy.
`pstree` draws the tree and the `f` option of `ps` adds the same ASCII tree.
`jobs` lists the jobs of the shell, and `ps -l` only gives a long format of a flat list.

questions.title: Star in a regular expression
questions.text: `notes` has three lines: `apple`, `banana` and `cherry`. In the shell, `ls a*` would list only the names that start with `a`. What does `grep 'a*' notes` print?

options.t: Only `apple`, the line that starts with `a`.
options.why: That is how the shell glob `a*` works; in a regular expression `*` repeats the previous character.

options.t: `apple` and `banana`, the lines that contain an `a`.
options.why: `a*` also matches zero `a`s, so lines without an `a` match too.
`a*` means "zero or more `a`", and zero `a`s matches in every line, so every line is selected.

options.t: Nothing, because `*` needs a character before it and `a*` is not valid.
options.why: It is valid: the star repeats the `a` before it.
The single quotes inside double quotes are kept as text, and the pair in the second word is literal too.
Inside single quotes nothing is expanded, so the second word keeps the double quotes and `$x`.
Word 1: the single quotes are text inside the double ones. Word 2: single quotes keep `"$x"` literal. Word 3: `\"` is a literal quote and `$x` expands.
The expansion happens in word 3 (double quotes) and not in word 2 (single quotes).

questions.title: Who is working and on what
questions.text: Which command lists the users who are logged in, what each one is running right now, and the load average of the machine?

options.why: It shows user, terminal and login time, but neither the running command nor the load.
Its header has the load average and each line has a WHAT column with the command of the user.
It shows past logins and logouts, not what is running now.
It prints the identity of the current user only.

questions.title: A hard link and rm
questions.text:
```
echo hi > f
ln f g
rm f
ls -l g
cat g
```
What do the last two commands show?

options.t: `ls -l g` shows a link count of 2, and `cat g` prints `hi`.
options.why: `rm f` removed a name, so the count went from 2 to 1.

options.t: `ls -l g` shows a link count of 0, and `cat g` fails.
options.why: The data stay while at least one name points to the inode.

options.t: `ls -l g` shows a link count of 1, and `cat g` prints `hi`.
options.why: The inode is the same; it lost one directory entry and keeps the other.

options.t: `ls -l g` shows a link count of 1, and `cat g` fails with "No such file or directory".
options.why: `g` is a full name for the inode, not a pointer to `f`.

options.t: `echo hi | tee t1` prints `hi` on the screen and also writes it to the file `t1`.
options.why: True: it copies stdin to stdout and to the files.

options.t: `ls | tee a b` writes the listing into both `a` and `b`.
options.why: True: `tee` accepts several files.

options.t: `echo new | tee t2` replaces the old content of the file `t2`, if it already existed.
options.why: True: without options it truncates the file.

options.t: In `ls | tee l.txt | wc -l`, `wc` gets nothing, as `tee` keeps the data.
options.why: False: `tee` passes everything to stdout too, so `wc` counts the lines and `l.txt` has the listing.

questions.title: Moving around in info
questions.text: You are reading a node of a manual with `info`. Which key takes you to its parent node, one level up?

options.why: It goes to the previous node of the same level.
It returns to the last page you read.
It moves up one level in the hierarchy of nodes.
It goes to the top page of the manual, not just one level up.

questions.title: Executable for the owner only
questions.text: `deploy.sh` has mode `rw-r--r--` and a correct shebang. Which command lets only its owner run `./deploy.sh`, without touching the other bits?

options.why: Without a letter before `+x` the execute bit goes to the owner, the group and the others (with the usual umask 022).
That gives execute to the others, not to the owner; the owner could not run it.
It adds only the owner's execute bit: the mode becomes `rwxr--r--`.
That removes execute for everyone; nobody had it, so nothing changes.

questions.title: Once per file
questions.text: The directory holds `a.log`, `sub/b.log` and `c.txt`. What does `find . -name '*.log' -exec echo file: {} \;` print?

options.why: That is what the `+` terminator does; with `\;` the command runs once for each file.
`{}` is replaced by the name of each file found.
The command is run once per match and `{}` stands for the path.

options.t: An error, because `-exec` cannot be used with `echo`.
options.why: Any command can follow `-exec`; the error appears only if the closing `\;` is missing.

questions.title: Brackets in a test
questions.text: Which statement about `if` and `[ ]` is FALSE?

options.why: True: that ends the structure.

options.t: `elif` lets a second condition be tested without nesting another `if`.
options.why: True: it is "else if".

options.t: In `[ $x -gt 3 ]` the spaces after `[` and before `]` are required.
options.why: True: `[` is a command and `]` its last argument.
False: without the space the shell looks for a command called `[5` and fails with "command not found".
